nameStory: The Saffron-winged Meadowhawk gets its name from the gorgeous golden-yellow wing stripes that shine like precious saffron spice in young dragonflies and females. Saffron, one of the world's most valuable spices, comes from crocus flowers and has that same warm, golden hue you'll see glinting on this dragonfly's wings as it patrols sunny meadows.
description: The Saffron-winged Meadowhawk is a medium-sized dragonfly with a slender yellowish-brown body that develops pale red coloring as it matures. Both males and females sport distinctive golden wing stripes when young, though these fade in older males. At about 1.4 inches long, it's a typical meadowhawk size with the characteristic habit of perching on low vegetation in open areas. The body features striking black triangular markings along the sides, and the legs are boldly striped in black and yellow or red.

idTips.label: Golden Wing Stripes
idTips.description: Look for saffron-colored (golden-yellow) stripes along the wings, especially visible in females and younger individuals - they catch the sunlight beautifully and feel smooth to the touch if you can examine a resting specimen closely

idTips.label: Black Side Triangles
idTips.description: Dark triangular markings run along the sides of the yellowish-brown abdomen like a row of tiny arrowheads pointing toward the tail

idTips.label: Striped Legs
idTips.description: The legs show bold black and yellow or red stripes that look almost like tiny candy canes - quite different from the solid-colored legs of many other dragonflies

idTips.label: Reddish Wing Veins
idTips.description: The network of veins running through the wings appears orange to reddish in color, creating a warm-toned roadmap across the clear wing membrane

idTips.label: Color-changing Body
idTips.description: The abdomen starts yellowish-brown but gradually develops pale red tones as the dragonfly matures - like a slow sunset happening over weeks

habitat: Saffron-winged Meadowhawks prefer open wetland areas including pond edges, marsh borders, and slow-moving streams with adjacent meadows or fields. They're often found perching on low shrubs, grasses, or fence posts near water where they can easily spot prey and potential mates. Look for them in areas where forest meets wetland, as they appreciate both the hunting grounds of open space and the shelter of nearby trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not typically active yet in early spring, as this species emerges later in the season than many dragonflies.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity begins in mid to late summer when fresh adults emerge from their aquatic larval stage and begin hunting and mating. Look for the brightest golden wing stripes during this time.
seasonality.fall: This is prime time for Saffron-winged Meadowhawks, as they remain active well into autumn when many other dragonflies have disappeared. Mature individuals show their best red coloring now.
seasonality.winter: Adults do not survive freezing temperatures, but larvae continue developing underwater beneath the ice, preparing for next year's emergence.

funFact: Unlike many dragonflies that die at the first frost, Saffron-winged Meadowhawks are cold-weather champions that can actually survive light frosts and continue flying on warm autumn days when temperatures climb back above 50°F - you might spot one hunting on a sunny October afternoon while wearing your winter coat!
confusionNotes: This species is notoriously difficult to distinguish from Ruby and White-faced Meadowhawks, especially as they age and lose their distinctive golden wing stripes. Memory trick: Remember 'Saffron = Stripes' - if you can see golden wing stripes on a meadowhawk, you're likely looking at a Saffron-winged, but if those stripes are absent or very faded, you'll need to look at other subtle features like face color and leg patterns.
contextualKnowledge: The meadowhawk group represents one of the trickiest identification challenges in North American dragonflies, with seven species in New England that can look remarkably similar. Many experienced dragonfly watchers rely on high-quality photographs and detailed field guides to separate these species confidently, so don't be discouraged if you find meadowhawk identification challenging at first.
compareHints: Among New England's meadowhawks, the Saffron-winged is most easily distinguished by its golden wing stripes in younger individuals and females, while the Ruby Meadowhawk typically shows clearer wings and the White-faced has a distinctly pale face. The Black Meadowhawk is much darker overall, and the Band-winged shows different wing markings, making the Saffron-winged's golden stripes your best identifying feature when present.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the seven meadowhawk species in New England, Autumn Meadowhawks are distinguished by their completely yellow legs - most other meadowhawks have black legs or black stripes on their legs.

Among New England meadowhawks, the band-winged is the only one with prominent dark wing bands - ruby meadowhawks have clear wings and bright red males, while autumn meadowhawks lack wing bands and have more orange-red coloring.
Among the seven meadowhawk species in New England, the white-faced is the only one where males develop a pure white face - other meadowhawks have reddish, yellowish, or dark faces.

Cherry-faced meadowhawks are distinguished from other meadowhawks primarily by their very dark red, almost burgundy faces when mature, compared to the brighter reds of ruby meadowhawks or the white faces of white-faced meadowhawks.
